summary:
Moscow Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where transgender visitors face severe legal and physical risk under a regime that has tightened sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" statute criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings state this directly to LGBT travellers.

The UK government's country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records the operative legal position: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the Russian constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression "promoting" non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 "extremism"-related convictions for participating in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its alleged symbols, alongside 81 people convicted of administrative offences across 98 court cases since January 2024, mostly for posts on social media. These federal enforcement mechanisms apply nationwide, Moscow Oblast included, and the 2023 Supreme Court designation opened criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison.

Entry and transit are already flagged at the highest level by foreign governments: the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed specifically at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Those raids illustrate the enforcement pattern reaching the metropolitan area adjoining Moscow Oblast, and they establish the expected tempo of any further operations.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
localsOnly:
Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and "extremism" prosecutions, according to the UK country policy and information note of June 2025. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, ending legal access to gender-affirming medical care for residents as well as visitors.

Human Rights Watch's count as of 30 June 2025 records 101 "extremism"-related convictions for participating in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its alleged symbols, plus 81 people convicted of administrative offences across 98 court cases since January 2024, mostly for displaying those symbols on social media. The designation itself was handed down by the Supreme Court in 2023, building on the 2013 "gay propaganda" law, and criminal charges under it carry up to 12 years in prison.

Residents seeking to leave Russia rely on the UK Home Office standard (country policy and information note v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026), which affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention and so may qualify for protection on that basis. The 2023 ban on legal gender change means residents cannot update birth certificates, passports or other official records to reflect their gender.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Moscow Oblast-level enforcement data appears in the source inventory. Every finding above derives from federal law or nationwide court reporting, and oblast-level police or court practice is not separately sourced; the record therefore describes the national framework as it applies within the oblast rather than oblast-specific operations.

The figure of a national model score of 0.12 attached to this record is a model estimate, not a sourced legal finding, and should not be read as evidence about conditions on the ground.

Whether Moscow Oblast authorities have conducted independent raids, inspections or prosecutions targeting LGBT venues or individuals is unresolved and not sourced here. The reported bar raids of January 2024 took place in the city of Moscow, which is administratively separate from Moscow Oblast.

Whether entry screening, passport gender markers or detention conditions specific to Moscow Oblast differ from the national position is not sourced; the inventory establishes national rules only, including the 2023 ban on document-based gender change and the detention risk for foreigners.
